Orihuela, a Spanish diocese covering Alicante province except Caudete and Ayora, centers on a city of 24,364 with an ancient see at Bigastro. James the Conqueror retook Orihuela from the Moors in 1265, gave it to Alfonso X, and restored its church under Cartagena.

Lost to Castile in 1304, it petitioned for its own bishop. It won a collegiate church from antipope Benedict XIII and a vicariate from Martin V, and gained a cathedral in 1510 under Cartagena. Only Philip II's settlement at Monzón in 1563 finally separated the diocese, and the entry lists its later bishops.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parenzo-pola:
Parenzo-Pola is a diocese on an Adriatic promontory, whose cathedral crowns the headland close to the water. First bishop Euphrasius built it under Justinian, when Byzantine building first reached the Adriatic shore, and it stands as Austria's best-kept monument of that age. Digging shows it is the newest of three churches, the second from Constantine's time and the oldest earlier still, proving Parenzo's ancient Christianity.

Parenzo stood alone from Euphrasius until union with Pola in 1827. Pola's first bishop, Venerius, died about 520. Today the united diocese, under Goerz, counts 132,000 Catholics, 135 secular priests, one monastery of 21 monks, and six or eight convents with 132 nuns. Sources include Kandler's Istrian diplomatic code and Cappelletti's churches of Italy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulinus-of-p:
Paulinus of Pella was a fifth-century Christian poet born at Pella in Macedonia to a Bordeaux family. Son of an official, which explains his Macedonian birth and childhood stay at Carthage, he soon went back to Bordeaux. He was probably grandson of the poet Ausonius. At eighty-three he composed his life account, the Eucharisticon, a thanksgiving framed as a diary.

Illness, lost property, and invasion dangers fill more of it than happy days, yet it offers a sincere picture of the age in lofty feeling. Style and versification do not always match its sincerity and inspiration. Its date is uncertain: a passage, altered in transmission, may point between 459 and 465. The single manuscript omits the author's name, known only through Margarin de La Bigne, who handled another manuscript naming Paulinus. Brandes printed the poem in 1888.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-arias-d:
Pedro Arias de Avila, also called Pedrarias Davila, was a Spanish knight from Segovia, born about 1450 and dead at Leon in 1530. He married a friend of Queen Isabella, whence his preferment, and saw service in Europe. At nearly seventy he was made commander in 1514 of the largest expedition sent to America. He reached Santa Marta with nineteen vessels and 1,500 men.

Thence he went to Darien, where Balboa, discoverer of the South Sea, governed. Pedrarias replaced him, married him to his daughter, and had him judicially murdered. In 1519 he founded Panama City. He joined the original pact with Pizarro and Almagro that led to Peru's discovery, but withdrew in 1526 for small compensation. That year he was replaced as Panama's governor and retired to Leon, dying past eighty. He left an unenviable record as unreliable, cruel, and unscrupulous, yet his Panama foundation laid the basis for Peru's conquest.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pella:
Pella was a Greek town east of the Jordan whose ruins still stand at Tabakat-Fahil. Founded by Macedonians and claimed by Alexander in local tradition, it passed from Alexander Jannaeus, who destroyed it, to Pompey, who rebuilt it and joined it to Syria. It then belonged to the Decapolis and marked the northern edge of Jewish Perea.

Its fame rests on the refuge it gave early Christians in 66, when the Jerusalem community fled there during the Jewish revolt under St. Simon. After the second revolt was crushed, some of its people returned to Mount Sion under Bishop Mark. Christianity still lasted at Pella, as tombs, inscriptions, and the writer Ariston show. The entry names only three of its bishops and notes its basilica and necropolis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-of-aqui:
Peter of Aquila, called Scotellus, was a Franciscan theologian and bishop, born at Aquila late in the thirteenth century. By 1334 he was master of theology and Franciscan provincial in Tuscany, then confessor to Queen Joan I of Naples and inquisitor at Florence. When civic authority punished his servants, he excommunicated the priors and laid the town under interdict.

In 1347 he became Bishop of S. Angelo de Lombardi, and in 1348 was transferred to Trivento, where he died in 1361. His reputation rests on interpretation of Duns Scotus, earning him the title Doctor sufficiens, the Sufficient Doctor. His commentaries on the four books of Sentences, a compendium of Scotus, were called the Scotellum, giving him his surname. They passed through editions from Speier in 1480 to Genoa in 1907.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pogla: Pogla is a titular see, a former bishopric kept in name, in Pamphylia Secunda. It is mentioned only by Ptolemy, and possibly by Hierocles under the form Socla, which likely means another place. Coins were struck with the pagan name pogleon. Today it is the town of Foughla near Adalia. Two bishops are known: Paul at Chalcedon in 451 and Nicephorus at Nicaea in 787. The see appears among the suffragans of Perge as late as the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-portiuncula:
Portiuncula is a town and parish about three-quarters of a mile from Assisi, with about two thousand people. It grew around Our Lady of the Angels basilica and its Franciscan monastery. Here on 24 February 1208 Francis of Assisi found his vocation. Here he mostly lived after Benedictines gave him the little chapel about 1211. Here he died on Saturday, 3 October 1226.

Portiuncula means a little portion of land. Legend says hermits from the Josaphat Valley built the chapel under Liberius and brought relics from the Virgin's grave, and that it passed to St Benedict in 516. It was called Our Lady of the Valley of Josaphat or of the Angels. Here the Franciscan Order was cradled, and dying Francis commended the chapel to his brothers' care. The Portiuncula Indulgence may be gained as often as one visits, and applies to souls in purgatory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rudolph-agric:
Rudolph Agricola, a humanist of the earlier period, energetically advanced classical study in Germany. Born at Bafflo near Groningen in 1442 or 1443, he died at Heidelberg on 28 October 1485. His family name was Huysmann. He studied the higher branches at Louvain, learning Cicero and Quintilian.

At Paris he worked with Heynlin von Stein and befriended John Reuchlin. Early in the seventies he went to Italy, joining humanists chiefly at Rome and Ferrara, winning renown for elegant Latin and knowledge of philosophy. After seven years in Italy he returned to Germany, rousing friends by person and letter for classical learning. Loving independence, he took no fixed post. In 1481 he spent six months at Brussels at Archduke Maximilian's court. Then he accepted Bishop John of Dalberg's invitation to Heidelberg, lecturing from 1482, studying Hebrew, and publishing a translation of the Psalms.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-galla:
Galla was a Roman widow of the sixth century, daughter of the younger Symmachus, a learned patrician whom Theodoric unjustly put to death in 525. Widowed before her first year of marriage ended, she founded a convent and hospital near Saint Peter's while still very young. She spent the rest of her days in austerity and works of mercy. Fulgentius of Ruspe's letter on the state of widows is thought to have been written to her.

Her church in Rome, by the Piazza Montanara, once housed an image of Our Lady. The picture reportedly showed a vision granted to Galla and was carried in procession in plague times. Regarded as miraculous, it now stands over the high altar of Santa Maria in Campitelli. Her feast is kept on 5 October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-gudula:
Gudula, born in seventh-century Brabant to Witger and Amalberga and dead early in the eighth century, grew up in a household steeped in piety and good works. Her mother embraced religious life after Gudula's birth. Her sister Reinelda and her brother Emebertus, later bishop of Cambrai, shared the devout atmosphere, and Gudula often walked two miles to the church at Moorzeele. She was buried at Ham in East Flanders.

About a century after her death her relics were moved to Moorzeele. Between 977 and 988 they were taken to the chapel of Saint Géry at Brussels, and in 1047 to the church of Saint-Michel. In 1579 the collegiate church was pillaged by heretics, and her relics were dug up and scattered. Brussels keeps her feast on 8 January and Ghent on 19 January, and she is pictured holding a candle and a lamp that a demon tries to put out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-petroni:
Petronilla, a virgin probably martyred at Rome near the end of the first century, is known chiefly through her tomb. Sixth- and seventh-century lists of martyrs' graves place her burial on the Via Ardeatina beside Nereus and Achilleus, and digs in the Catacomb of Domitilla confirmed those notices. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows the archaeology rather than the legend.

A church built into the catacomb once held all three tombs, and a painting shows Petronilla welcoming a dead woman named Veneranda into heaven. Later tales made her the daughter of Peter the apostle, but the entry treats that link as pious fiction. Readers interested in early Roman martyr cults will find the hard evidence separated cleanly from the stories that grew around it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sancho-de-avi:
Sancho de Ávila, born at Ávila in Old Castile in 1546 and named for his birthplace, died at Plasencia on 6 or 7 December 1625. From a distinguished family, he stood out still more for holiness, vast learning, and success as a preacher. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia sketches a bishop-scholar of Spain's golden age.

He studied and took his doctorate at Salamanca, then held in turn the sees of Murcia, Jaén in Andalusia, Sigüenza, from 1615, and Plasencia from 1622 until his death. He had served as confessor to Teresa of Ávila. His Spanish works include a 1611 treatise on honouring saints' bodies and relics and sermons printed at Baeza in 1615. He also translated the Sighs of St Augustine and left manuscript lives of Augustine and Thomas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-lucia-d: Santa Lucia del Mela is a prelature nullius, a district with its own prelate but no bishop of its own, lying within the archdiocese of Messina in Sicily. It is now ruled by an administrator apostolic who always holds a titular bishopric. It comprises seven parishes served by seventy-two secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santiago-de-g:
Santiago de Guatemala, an archdiocese matching the republic of Guatemala in Central America, spans 28,950 square miles between Mexico, Belize, Honduras, El Salvador, and the Pacific. Paul III made it a diocese on 18 December 1534, with Francisco Marroquín, who had sailed with the governor Pedro de Alvarado, as first bishop. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists a long episcopal line.

Marroquín's successors run through Villalpando, Fernández de Córdova, Ramírez de Arellano, Cabezas Altamirano, Zapata y Sandoval, and a dozen more to the modern archbishops. The entry sets out the archdiocese's bounds, its parishes, and its place in a republic where the Church shaped schools and public life from the conquest onward. Readers tracing Central American church history start here.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-satala:
Satala, a titular see in Armenia Prima suffragan of Sebasteia, lay in a mountain-ringed valley a little north of the Euphrates, where the road from Trapezus to Samosata crossed Rome's frontier. Later two highways linked it with Nicopolis. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a legionary camp that became a town.

The site was likely occupied when Vespasian annexed Lesser Armenia. Trajan visited in 115, received homage from Caucasus and Black Sea princes, and probably stationed the Fifteenth Legion Apollinaris there, building the great permanent camp it held until the fifth century. A town grew around the camp, already important by Ptolemy's time. Persians lost a battle beneath its walls in 530, Justinian strengthened its defences, yet Persians captured it in 607. Today it is Sadagh village.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simla:
Simla, an archdiocese in India newly created by Pius X in a decree of 13 September 1910, was formed by cutting portions from the Archdiocese of Agra and the Diocese of Lahore. Simla itself, the metropolitan city, took the Church of Saints Michael and Joseph as pro-cathedral. From Agra came Ambala, Hissar, Karnal, Patiala, Nabha, Sind, Loharu, and Maler Kotla. From Lahore came Mandi, Suket, Kulu, Lahul, and Spiti. Suffragans were reserved for the future by the Holy See.

As the two older dioceses belonged to Italian and Belgian Capuchin Franciscans, the new archdiocese went to the same fathers of the English province. Its first archbishop was Anselm Kenealy, known in England as a logic and metaphysics lecturer, guardian of Crawley monastery, and provincial of the English province. Consecrated at Rome on 1 January 1911, he sailed for India that April and was welcomed with an imposing reception.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-andrew-bob:
St. Andrew Bobola was a Polish Jesuit martyr, born of an old and illustrious family in the palatinate of Sandomir in 1590 and dead at Janow on 16 May 1657. This entry follows a novice at Wilno in 1611, ordained in 1622, preacher at St. Casimir's in Wilno, and after solemn vows in 1630, superior at Bobruisk, where his preaching worked wonders and his devotion shone during a plague epidemic.

From 1636 he laboured in the Lithuanian missions while Cossacks, Russians, and Tatars ravaged Poland and Protestants and schismatics attacked the Catholic faith together. His success in converting schismatics drew the rage of men in high places, and the entry follows him toward the martyrdom that his missionary triumphs provoked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-attala:
St. Attala was born in Burgundy in the sixth century and died in 627. This entry follows a monk who first entered Lerins, but left, displeased with the loose discipline there. He entered Luxeuil, the monastery just founded by St. Columban. After King Theodoric II expelled Columban from Luxeuil, Attala was to succeed him as abbot. He preferred to follow him into exile.

They settled on the banks of the Trebbia, a little north-east of Genoa, where they founded the celebrated abbey of Bobbio. After Columban's death in 615, Attala took over as Bobbio's abbot. He and his monks endured many hardships under the Arian king Ariowald. As abbot, Attala demanded strict discipline, and when many monks rebelled, calling his discipline too rigorous, he let them leave the monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fabiola:
Fabiola, a Roman matron of the patrician Fabia family, turned a scandalous past into a life of public penance and charity. Married first to a vicious husband, she divorced him under Roman law and, against church ordinance, married again before his death. On the Easter eve after her second husband's death, she appeared at the Lateran gates in penitential dress and did public penance. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death to 27 December 399 or 400.

Under Jerome's influence she gave herself to asceticism and the sick, nursing even those with repulsive wounds. At Bethlehem she studied Scripture under Jerome in Paula's hospice, then returned to Rome after Hun raids and the Origen quarrel. With the senator Pammachius she built a great pilgrims' hospice at Porto. Her funeral showed Rome's gratitude, and Jerome wrote her memoir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-felix-of-n:
Felix of Nola, a third-century priest of Naples, is remembered for prison escapes, a spider's web, and a refused bishopric. After his father's death he gave almost all his goods to the poor and was ordained by Maximus, bishop of Nola. When Decius's persecution broke out in 250, Maximus fled, and Felix was scourged, chained, and jailed. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 tells how an angel freed him to aid his speechless, starving bishop.

Hunted again, he hid in a hole whose mouth a spider webbed over, deceiving his pursuers. Six months in a dry well followed before the persecution eased and he resumed his duties. On Maximus's death the people wanted Felix as bishop, but he persuaded them to choose his senior in the priesthood. The entry joins marvels to modesty: a confessor who would not take the chair.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-finnian-of:
Finnian of Movilla, founder of a famous school about 540, is remembered through his pupil Columba and a stolen psalter. Born about 495, he studied under Colman of Dromore and Mochae of Noendrum, then at Candida Casa, Whithern, and in Rome. Returning to Ireland in 540, he brought a complete copy of Jerome's Vulgate. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 589.

At Movilla in County Down his most distinguished pupil was Columba, whose secret copying of the psalter led to a remarkable sequel. What survives of that copy, with its casket, rests in Dublin's National Museum as the Cathach, or Battler, once carried by O'Donnells into battle. Finnian also wrote a monastic rule and a penitential code. The entry joins schoolmaster, book, and battle relic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-of:
Francis of Paula, founder of the Minims, was a child of prayer whose parents' long childlessness ended through Francis of Assisi's intercession. Born at Paula in Calabria in 1416, eldest of three, he suffered in the cradle a swelling that threatened one eye. His parents vowed he would spend a year in St. Francis's little habit, and the child was cured at once. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Plessis in France to 2 April 1507.

At thirteen, warned by a vision of a Franciscan friar, he entered a Franciscan convent to fulfil his parents' vow. There his love of prayer and mortification edified all around him. The entry's opening chapters show sanctity forming early: a prayed-for son, a healed eye, and a boy keeping a vow in a friar's habit. From those beginnings grew the Minim order he would found.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gerard-maj:
Gerard Majella, Redemptorist brother who died at twenty-nine, bound himself by an extra vow to always choose the more perfect thing. Born at Muro, south of Naples, in April 1726, he lost his father Dominic while still a child. Poverty apprenticed him to a tailor whose foreman treated him cruelly, though his master loved him. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 16 October 1755.

Reverence for priests and love of suffering led him to serve a hard-to-please prelate, then return to tailoring, dividing earnings among his mother, the poor, and offerings for souls in purgatory. After failed attempts to become Franciscan and hermit, he entered the Redemptorists in 1749 and professed two years later, adding his vow of the more perfect. Leo XIII beatified him in 1893, and Pius X canonized him in 1904.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ignatius-l:
Ignatius Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, turned a soldier courtier into a pilgrim and organizer. He was baptized Iñigo in 1491 at Loyola castle above Azpeitia. He was youngest son of Beltrán de Oñez y Loyola and Marina Saenz. Raised in Juan Velásquez de Cuellar's household, he attended Ferdinand and Isabella's court in his suite. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Rome to 31 July 1556.

Conversion remade him, and notes from his early spiritual life grew into the little book of the Spiritual Exercises. Sicknesses in a public hospital, where friends tended him, became occasions for teaching prayer. His Paris companions, Favre, Xavier, and others, joined his project. The bull Regimini militantis Ecclesiae of 27 September 1540 sanctioned the Society, capped at sixty members. In April 1541, despite reluctance, he was elected first general.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ludmilla:
Ludmilla, grandmother of Wenceslaus, was strangled with her own veil at Tetin in 921. Born at Mielnik about 860, wife of Boriwoi, first Christian duke of Bohemia, she was baptized with her husband, probably by Methodius, in 871. Pagan fanatics drove them out, but they were soon recalled, reigned seven more years, then resigned for their son Spitignev and retired to Tetin. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates her death at Tetin to 15 September 921.

Spitignev died two years later, and Wratislaw, another son, succeeded, marrying Drahomira, a pretended Christian and secret favourer of paganism. Their twin sons were Wenceslaus and Boleslaus the Cruel, and Wenceslaus lived beside Ludmilla at Tetin. Wratislaw died in 916, leaving eight-year-old Wenceslaus successor. Jealous of Ludmilla's influence over the boy, Drahomira set two noblemen to murder her. First buried at Tetin's St. Michael's, her remains moved to Prague's St. George's before 1100.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paula:
Paula, a Roman widow of the first families of Rome, followed Jerome to Bethlehem and built monasteries there. Born in 347 and widowed at thirty-two in 379, she became through Marcella's circle a model of Christian widowhood. Her decisive meeting with Jerome came in 382, when he reached Rome with Epiphanius and Paulinus of Antioch.

Paula and her daughter Eustochium mastered Hebrew, aiming less at knowledge than at Christian perfection. She married her daughter Paulina to Senator Pammachius, buried Blesilla and Rufina, and sailed east with Eustochium. At Bethlehem she raised convents and a hospice beside Jerome's monastery. She died there in 404, honoured as a founder of Latin monastic life in the Holy Land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-o:
Paulinus of Nola, a Roman aristocrat turned monk bishop, traded wealth for a shrine town in Campania. Born at Bordeaux about 354 and schooled by the poet Ausonius, he governed Campania before marriage to the Christian Therasia and friendship with Martin of Tours turned him toward the faith. Baptised with his brother by Delphinus of Bordeaux, he lost his only child days after birth.

He and Therasia withdrew from the world, went to Spain, and were pressed into ordination at Barcelona in 394 or 395. Settling at Nola, he built an avenue and hospital beside the tomb of Felix, wrote poems and letters, and became bishop. He died on 22 June 431, leaving a rich correspondence with Augustine, Jerome, and Sulpicius Severus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-teresa-of-:
Teresa of Avila, reformer of Carmel and Doctor of the Church, turned a convent of one hundred and forty nuns into a movement of prayer. Born Teresa Sánchez Cepeda Dávila y Ahumada at Avila on 28 March 1515, third child of Alonso Sánchez de Cepeda, she lost her mother at fourteen. Schooled by Augustinian nuns, she left through illness and read Jerome's Letters with an uncle.

Against her father's will she entered the Carmelite Convent of the Incarnation in November 1535, a wrench she compared to death. Her father yielded at once. After profession she fell gravely ill, recovered through prayer, and began the mystical life recorded in her Life. She founded the Discalced Carmelites, wrote the Interior Castle and the Way of Perfection, and died at Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-thecla:
Thecla, Benedictine abbess of Kitzingen and Ochsenfurt, carried English monastic life into Germany with Boniface. Her birth date is unknown, and she died at Kitzingen about 790 or later. Boniface kept close correspondence with Wimborne in Dorset, and from Abbess Tetta in 748 and 749 he obtained colonies of nuns for Germany.

Among them, Thecla, kinswoman of Lioba, stood out for sanctity and learning. She lived under Lioba at Tauberbischofsheim until Boniface made her abbess of the new house at Ochsenfurt. On the death of Adelheid, foundress of Kitzingen, she was called to rule there too, keeping both abbeys. Martyrologies honour her on 15 October, others on 27 or 28 September. Her name may hide in Kitzingen's lists as Heilga, the saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-thecla:
Thecla of Iconium, reputed pupil of Paul, leads this entry on several saints of the name. All knowledge of her comes from the apocryphal Acts of Paul and Thecla, written about 180. Converted by Paul's preaching, she vowed perpetual virginity, survived the stake by miracle, survived wild beasts at Antioch, and died at Seleucia.

With Paul's consent she preached as a female apostle, and the entry allows that a real Iconian convert may stand behind the legend. Her cult spread widely in East and West, earning her the title apostle and protomartyr among women. Shorter notices cover other Theclas, including one of Aquileia kept on 3 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-vitalis-a:
Vitalis and Agricola were martyred at Bologna about 304, in the Diocletian persecution. Agricola, loved for his gentleness, converted his slave Vitalis to Christianity, and the two grew deeply attached. Vitalis suffered first, executed in the amphitheatre, while tortures and flattery failed to win Agricola, who was crucified at last.

Both were buried in the Jewish graveyard. In 393 Ambrose and Bishop Eusebius of Bologna moved their remains to a church, and Ambrose carried blood, cross, and nails to Florence, to the church built by the widow Juliana. His oration on that occasion is the only authority for their lives. Their feast is 4 November, and relics reached Rouen and Nola in 396.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sufetula:
Sufetula was a titular see of North Africa, apparently the Suthul where Jugurtha stored his treasures. Its Latin name is a diminutive of Sufes, a small town twenty-five miles further north, and under Rome it became a colony. In 647 it served as capital of the Byzantine patrician Gregory, who declared himself independent and was killed in battle with the Arabs, who stormed and pillaged the town.

Martyrs listed under Sufetula on 30 August seem to belong rather to Sufes. Only three bishops are known: Privatian at Carthage in 255, Jucundus at Carthage in 411 and 419, and Praesidius, scourged and exiled by Huneric in 484. Today the place is the village of Sbeitha in Tunisia, rich in Roman ruins, temples, churches, and Christian sculpture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thyrsus-gonza:
Thyrsus Gonzalez de Santalla, theologian and thirteenth general of the Society of Jesus, was born at Arganda, Spain, in 1624 and died at Rome in 1705. He entered the Society in March 1643, taught philosophy and theology at Salamanca, and spent the middle years preaching. In 1687, on his way to convert Muslims in Africa, he was sent as an elector to the general congregation, which chose him general that July.

As a young theologian Gonzalez had fought probabilism, the view that one may follow a merely probable opinion, and defended the stricter probabiliorism. His book on the subject was refused publication in 1674, but Innocent XI encouraged him, and the Holy Office in 1680 allowed Jesuits to defend probabiliorism. As general he pressed his own view among his subjects, printing a revised book at Dillingen in 1691 that his assistants kept from publication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tlaxcala:
Tlaxcala was a former diocese of New Spain, the fifth founded in the Americas and the second in Mexico. Its first acting bishop was the Dominican Julian Garces, named by Clement VII at Charles V's request. First presented as Bishop of Yucatan, Garces chose Tlaxcala itself as his cathedral town, reaching New Spain in 1527 and taking possession of his see.

Finding only a thatched altar at Tlaxcala and no cathedral, he moved the chapter to Puebla de los Angeles. A fine three-naved church stood there, and he transferred the see there on 3 October 1539. The entry follows later bishops, including Palafox's successor Osorio, viceroy of Mexico in 1664, and Labastida, driven out in the reform era. It also notes the great pyramid of Cholula, crowned by a church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tommaso-campa:
Tommaso Campanella, Dominican philosopher and writer, was baptized Giovanni Domenico at Stilo, Calabria, in 1568 and died at Paris in 1639. A ready writer of prose and verse at thirteen, he joined the Dominicans before fifteen, drawn by Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas. He defended the naturalist Telesio in his first work, Philosophia Sensibus Demonstrata, published at Naples in 1590.

His ardent temper and attacks on Aristotle brought him before the Holy Office, which held him until 1597. In September 1599 he was seized as head of a plot against Spanish rule in Naples. He was charged with heresy and with aiming at a communistic commonwealth, and put to torture by a political court. He survived, kept writing in prison, and died at Paris in 1639. His theory of being as power, wisdom and love runs through his wide-ranging writings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tudela:
A diocese in Spain whose city, of 9,213 people, was taken from the Moors by Alfonso el Batallador in March 1115. In 1121 the king gave the mosque and the tithes of several towns to Tudela's prior and chapter. He built Santa María, where Canons Regular of Saint Augustine settled under the abbot and prior.

The priory became a deanery in 1238, and in the sixteenth century its deans gained the use of pontificalia. Rivalry with the bishops of Tarazona and royal discontent over appointments led to the erection of the diocese by Pius VI in 1783. Francisco Ramón de Larumbe became first bishop in 1784.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-university-of:
The University of Alcalá may be said to have begun in the thirteenth century, when Sancho IV of Castile planned a Studium Generale at Alcalá de Henares. On 20 May 1293 he gave the Archbishop of Toledo, Gonzalo Gudiel, full powers to carry the plan out, though what came of the effort is unknown. On 16 July 1459 Pius II allowed Archbishop Alonso Carrillo to set up chairs where grammar and the liberal arts would be taught on set days.

Even then theology and canon law seem not to have been established, and grammar got only fitful teaching in the Franciscan convent of San Diego. Proper credit for founding the university goes to Cardinal Cisneros, whose story the entry goes on to tell, with the college's growth, its faculties, and its scholars. Readers trace here the slow birth of one of Spain's great seats of learning.

Upsala is the oldest and most celebrated university of Sweden, and its buildings still show it as a creation of the Catholic Church. The venerable Gothic cathedral holds in a silver reliquary the remains of St Eric the King, who died in 1161. It stands ringed by colleges, houses of the nations, hospitals, an observatory, and a library. A proposal to bring foreign scholars to Upsala for lectures is said to have been made at the church synod of Arboga in 1417.

It is certain that the Synod of Söderköping in 1441 charged the bishops to seek a studium generale. Shortly after, Denmark moved to found a university at Copenhagen, which spurred Archbishop Jakob Ulfsson, primate of Sweden, to act. The entry follows the foundation, the Reformation's transformation of the school, and its growth into Sweden's leading university, still gathered around its medieval cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-upsala:
Upsala in Sweden was a centre of heathen worship long before Christianity reached the north. When St Ansgar, Apostle of the North, came to Sweden in 829, the Swedes still kept sacrificial groves and idol temples. The most famed stood at Upsala, in what is now Old Upsala, the heart of idol worship not only for Sweden but for all Scandinavia. Even after Christianity spread, heathen sacrifices continued there.

The Bishops' Chronicle of Adam of Bremen, written between 1072 and 1076, describes the temple and its great feast every ninth year. All Sweden's provinces kept that feast in common, and none might stay away. The entry traces the temple's fame, the coming of Christianity, and the rise of the Christian see at Upsala, where a cathedral at last replaced the grove and its rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-usilla:
Usilla was a titular see of Byzacena in Africa, a city whose history is wholly unknown. Ptolemy mentions it, and the Peutinger Tables, with spelling variations, call it a municipality. Other ancient geographies place it thirty-two miles from Thysdrus, today El Djem, and twenty-eight miles from Thaenae, today Benshir Tina. Its ruins are known as Inshilla, among them the remains of a Byzantine basilica.

Six bishops of Usilla are named. Felix appears at Carthage in 256 and Cassianus at Carthage in 349. Theodore, a Donatist partisan of Maximianus, condemned Primianus at Cabarsussi in 393 and was himself condemned at Bagai in 394. The entry lists the remaining bishops and the see's later mentions, a brief record of a North African town known mostly through its bishops' names.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venezuela:
Venezuela is treated here as a South American republic, its geography, history, and Catholic life surveyed at length. Formed from the Spanish captaincy general of the same name, it covers some 280,918 square miles between the Caribbean, Brazil, British Guiana. Colombia, with mountain ranges, plains, great rivers led by the Orinoco, and lakes Maracaibo and Valencia.

After the physical survey the entry follows the country's political story and, at length, its church history, including the strained relations between Caracas governments and archbishops in the nineteenth century. One episode shows an archbishop deferring a thanksgiving Te Deum after a bloody victory until a promised amnesty took effect. So that church rejoicing would not coincide with families mourning the dead and imprisoned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-veruela:
Veruela is a celebrated Cistercian monastery and church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin, five miles northwest of Borja in Saragossa, Spain. Founded in 1146 by Pedro de Atarés, to whom the Virgin appeared and directed him to a hidden statue of herself. The monastery and church form one edifice whose building took more than twenty years.

The statue still stands venerated in the chapel. Its most famous abbots were Fernando de Aragón, nominated by Charles V in 1537 and later Archbishop of Saragossa. Lope Marco, who, his epitaph boasts, raised the monastery from earth to marble and from narrow to ample. The chapter house on the cloister's south side, Byzantine in style, is described as an exact copy of Westminster's cloister. The whole complex, built in differing styles, stands within a feudal-era wall.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viterbo-and-t:
Viterbo and Toscanella form a united diocese in central Italy. Its city standing at the foot of Monte Cimino in farm country and largely preserving its medieval character, above all in encircling walls still in good repair. Its oldest building, St Lawrence's cathedral, altered in the twelfth and sixteenth centuries, holds column capitals, two monuments of John XXI, frescoes.

Framed pictures, while the episcopal palace on its square, sculpted in the thirteenth century, hosted conclaves electing Gregory X, John XXI, and Martin IV. Other churches tell the city's story. The former Servite church of Verità is now a museum with Lorenzo da Viterbo's Espousals of the Virgin. Later sections follow Viterbo's revolts against papal rule, the tyranny of Francesco di Vico, killed by the people in 1387, and its return to Urban VI.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zela:
Zela is the Asia Minor titular see, suffragan of Amasea in the Helenopontus. On the eminence at the city's middle stood a famous temple, consecrated by Persian kings to their national divinities Anahita, Vohu-Mano, and Anadates. Zela is famous for Mithridates Eupator's victory over Valerius Trianus, Lucullus's lieutenant, in 67 B.C., and for Caesar's victory over Pharnaces in 47 B.C., after which he wrote, I came, I saw, I conquered.

At first a mere hamlet, Zela gained city rank from Pompey and became capital of a district allotted to Queen Pythadoris. It passed to Nero with all Pontus Polemoniacus by its last king and stayed Greco-Roman until the Turks seized it in 1397. Le Quien names bishops Heraclius at Nicaea in 325, Atticus at Chalcedon in 451, Hyperechius in 458, Georgius in 692, Constantine in 787, and Paul in 879. Zela, now Zile, holds 20,000 people, 5,000 of them Christians.
copyright-law-of-the-united-states-of-am:
The United States Copyright Office's Circular 92 prints the copyright law of the United States as contained in Title 17 of the United States Code. The contents open with the constitutional provision that empowers Congress to secure authors' rights for limited times. The chapters then build the whole federal scheme: subject matter and scope, ownership and transfer, duration, notice, deposit and registration, infringement and remedies, importation, and the Copyright Office itself. Later chapters cover licensing, the Copyright Royalty Judges, and protection for vessel hull designs and semiconductor chips.

Unlike a treatise, the circular offers the statute's own words, organized for working use by authors, publishers, and lawyers. Its preface explains the codification and its amendments. Readers get the primary text of American copyright here entire: the law that decides what may be copied, for how long, and what it costs to take what the law reserves.

dracula:
Bram Stoker, an Irish theatre man, wrote this famed novel of the vampire in 1897. He built it from years of notes on lore, maps, and the old tales of the Carpathians. The Count at its heart has since become the most known figure in all horror.

The tale is told in letters, diaries, and news cuts, a form Stoker handles with great skill. Count Dracula comes from his keep in Transylvania to England, and Van Helsing leads the hunt back. The book fixed the rules of the vampire for the modern mind, from fangs to stakes.
emile-zola:
William Dean Howells wrote this appraisal of Emile Zola within weeks of the French novelist's death, arguing that modern speed lets readers judge a writer fairly almost at once. Zola's great epical imagination and ethical force, he says, were already clear while he lived. The essay defends the dead man against easy moral horror.

Howells examines Zola's naturalist creed, the claim to portray fact without choice or limitation, and shows that Zola always chose and limited, as even a map does. That delusion, he argues, caused endless misunderstanding of the novels. The piece captures an American realist measuring a French master, respectfully correcting his theory while honoring his power and honesty.
farewell-nikola: Farewell, Nikola, Guy Boothby's Dr. Nikola finale. The villain's farewell. This book preserves that novel. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBILiuzzoViola_:
Paul Magnusson reported for the Washington Post that relatives of Viola Liuzzo had filed a two-million-dollar wrongful-death claim against the FBI. Liuzzo was a civil rights worker who was slain in the South. Her family placed legal blame for her death at the Bureau's door.

A claim of that size against a federal agency is an accusation in legal form. It says the family's lawyers believed the FBI bore responsibility, not just the men who fired. Magnusson's article preserves the filing as the public first heard it, one step in the family's long fight over her killing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JohnsonPriscill:
A magazine printed Part II of an excerpt from Twenty Letters to a Friend, the forthcoming memoir of Svetlana Alliluyeva. She was Stalin's daughter, and the magazine billed the pages as her intimate recollections. The excerpt is filed in this archive under the name Priscilla Johnson.

Alliluyeva's defection to the West was a sensation, and her memoir promised the dictator's home life from inside the family. Magazines excerpted it in parts to feed that appetite. The pages preserved here are the second installment, Stalin remembered by the daughter who had escaped him.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KaiserRobertBla:
Steven V. Roberts wrote about Robert Blair Kaiser and the literary negotiations around Sirhan Sirhan. His piece opens on election night, with Kaiser keeping vigil while Robert Kennedy's fate hung in the balance. From that night it moves to the business that followed: books, rights, and the men bargaining over a killer's story.

An assassination creates a market before it creates a history. Kaiser's negotiations put a price on access to Sirhan, and Roberts examines the dealing in plain view. The piece preserves the publishing scramble that began while the country was still in mourning.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MumfordPamelaLi:
FBI Special Agent Chester C. Orton interviewed Pamela Lillian Mumford on February 24, 1964. Mumford identified Albert Osborne as the man who had sat next to Lee Harvey Oswald on a bus. The bus ran from Nuevo Laredo to Mexico City in the fall of 1963. Osborne also used the name John Howard Bowen.

Oswald's Mexico trip was one of the most investigated journeys in the case. Who sat beside him, and what was said, mattered to agents tracing his contacts. Mumford's identification put a named man in the next seat. The interview preserves her account in the bureau's standard form, one witness statement among thousands gathered that winter.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaysSurveillanc: The Rays surveillance file: a declassified US government document at the Internet Archive, titled but not described. Whose surveillance, and when, the catalog leaves unsaid. The file's text has not reached the public. A labeled folder with its papers missing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WilliamsonDougl: Douglas Williamson gives his name to the title of this declassified US government document, via the Internet Archive. No year, no agency, no abstract accompanies it. Public text not located. One more name in the declassified set.
ideala:
Sarah Grand's Ideala is a novel of a strong-minded woman thinking her way through marriage, society and belief. Grand warns readers not to take Ideala's opinions as final, since much of what she thinks is only a strong mind bubbling through change.

The preface traces that fermentation through three stages: the vinous (excitable), acetous (embittered) and putrefactive (unwholesome) stages. Even at its worst, Grand insists, Ideala's mind is earnest and seeks truth diligently, stumbling on good and bad together. The novel suits readers interested in early feminist fiction, and in a heroine who is deliberately transitional, repulsive at times, but never indifferent.
journal-of-a-west-india-proprietor-kept-:
Matthew Gregory Lewis's Journal of a West India Proprietor records his residences in Jamaica in 1815-16 and 1817. Lewis, author of The Monk, died at sea on the voyage home in 1818. The journals were printed from his manuscript in 1834. Entries run from November 1815 into January 1818.

The book opens with the voyage out, a dingy wait at an inn at Gravesend, and the ship's delayed sailing. Lewis writes as a planter inspecting his own estates and the enslaved people who worked them. His daily notes mix weather, society, illness, and estate business. Historians read the journal for its close, uneasy picture of Jamaican plantation life before emancipation.
lyra-frivola:
Lyra Frivola is a book of light verse by A. D. Godley, printed in 1900. This second edition gathers pieces from the St James's Gazette and Oxford Magazine. Godley was an Oxford don with a gift for comic Latin and English rhyme. The contents promise a Rubáiyát of Moderations and verses after Horace.

Poems here treat journalists abroad, Christmas thoughts, and the paradise of lecturers. Oxford life supplies jokes on degrees, schools, and dons. One piece answers a match against Newnham, the women's college. Godley's wit is dry, learned, and never heavy. The book is a fine sample of the don's art of nonsense verse.
marcella:
Marcella is a novel by Mrs. Humphry Ward, published in two volumes in 1894. Ward had already won fame with Robert Elsmere. She inscribed this book to her father in love and gratitude. It opens with Marcella Boyce kneeling at a window in delight.

Before her stretch a broad lawn and old trees, shaped by centuries. Marcella takes pleasure with a passionate intensity that rules her life. She is young, ardent, and full of new ideas about the poor. Her story brings her into conflict with landowners and custom. Ward writes of faith, duty, and social reform. Marcella stands among her most powerful heroines of ideas.
nasa-tm-19660022437-low-speed-measuremen:
John W Paulson measured unsteady sideways behavior of a model bomber in Langley's free-flight tunnel. The model had a sixty-degree delta wing. The airplane it copies carries four pod-mounted jet engines. A large droppable pod under it holds the warhead and some fuel, the introduction says. Tests ran with that pod fitted and removed, and with the vertical tail fitted and removed.

Paulson sought the rolling, yawing, and sideslipping measures that govern sideways stability. In general, he found that frequency had little effect on the values up to about twenty degrees of attack. Rolling and yawing results differed only slightly between the two main layouts. Free-flight models reveal unsteady behavior that fixed tunnel models can miss.
nasa-tm-19670008868-enumerating-neighbor:
A. V. M. Ferris-Prabhu, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, writes about crystal geometry in this note. His subject is the diamond-like lattice, the pattern atoms form in diamond and similar materials. The practical question is simple to state: for any atom in the pattern, where are its neighbors?

An earlier paper gave a method for counting neighbors in certain lattices. Ferris-Prabhu offers a considerably simpler method for diamond-like ones. His method exploits the symmetry of the lattice. He treats the pattern as two interlocking face-centered sublattices and gives the vectors that locate sites on each.
nasa-tm-19670019471-multiple-midcourse-m:
Abolghassem Ghaffari, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this guidance paper in June 1966. It treats multiple midcourse maneuvers in interplanetary guidance, the small engine firings that correct a spacecraft's course between planets. Ghaffari investigates how many such corrections a mission needs, and where along the flight they should fall.

The test case is a flyby mission to Jupiter with a spin-stabilized spacecraft. Its goals were to pass within about a million kilometers of the planet, roughly six Jupiter diameters, after a flight of five hundred days. Applying the spacing-ratio method, Ghaffari found that one constant spacing ratio for the velocity sensitivity gave a near-optimum spacing of correction times. Charts and figures lay out the Earth-Jupiter transfer geometry, the trajectory near Jupiter, and a guidance chart for the transfer.
nasa-tm-19680017360-dampers-to-suppress-:
Wilmer H. Reed III and Rodney L. Duncan of Langley Research Center survey dampers against wind-driven shaking in this paper, presented in August 1967. Tall, flexible structures such as stacks, antennas, and erected launch vehicles can oscillate in ground winds. Unchecked motion threatens both the structure and nearby work.

Wind tunnel studies with an aeroelastic model of the Saturn V led to viscous dampers on the full-scale vehicle. Those dampers guarded against excessive ground wind oscillations before launch. A simpler damper, chains hanging in containers, eased shaking on a U.S. Navy antenna system. The paper also reports progress on other damper work at Langley.
nasa-tm-19690010452-an-approach-to-optim:
Optimum loading of a solar array under temperature changes is this thesis's subject. It is a master's thesis in electrical engineering at the University of Virginia. A solar array gives its best power only at the right operating point. Heat shifts that point, so a fixed load wastes part of the array on every orbit.

The author works one Earth-orbiting mission under stated power limits, sizing its array two ways. A constant-current battery charging scheme is compared against a taper-current scheme. The taper design, the thesis shows, uses the array better: smaller area, lighter weight, and lower cost. Control is the key, adjusted smoothly against array temperature and in steps against experiment power demand.
nasa-tm-19690018711-nickel-cadmium-batte:
G. Halpert of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote volume three of the Nickel-Cadmium Battery Test Project in March 1969, numbered X-735-69-25. Aerospace batteries were cycled under related schemes at Martin Marietta's Baltimore Division. The project asked how the way a battery is worked governs how long it lives, and how it finally fails.

When half a battery's cells failed, technicians opened the rest and analyzed plates and separators. One long-term decay mode proved common to every battery, whatever its working scheme. Electrolyte crept into the plates, drying the separator out. Negative material then grew through the separator and glued it fast to the negative plates. Chemical, thermal, and structural measurements document the slow failure in detail.
nasa-tm-19690028458-flight-performance-o:
Lewis Research Center reports the Atlas-Agena flight that launched ATS-3 in this memorandum. Three Applications Technology Satellites flew on Atlas-Agena vehicles for experiments in communications, cloud cover photography, and spacecraft environment studies. The ATS-3 flight took place in November 1967.

Coverage runs from lift-off through the Agena reorientation maneuver. Eugene E. Coffey and Richard P. Geye describe the launch vehicle itself. George J. Schaefer and James C. Stoll present the trajectory plan and results phase by phase. Phases include Atlas booster, sustainer, and vernier flight, plus both Agena burns. The ATS-3 flight concluded the Atlas-Agena missions of the program.
nasa-tm-19690030506-nasa-s-efforts-in-pr:
G. T. McCoy, NASA's Deputy Assistant General Counsel for Patent Matters, explained the agency's new data clauses for software in this talk. He gave it at a Software Protection Workshop on June 4, 1969. The setting was a wider conference on copyright for programs built by NASA and Defense Department contractors.

McCoy walks through NASA's proposed regulations line by line, noting small wording changes as he goes. The rules were drafted from hard experience, he says, recognizing the several ways software can be protected. They also had to serve NASA's own needs as a buyer. He answers one break-time charge head on: the proposals were not intended as a wipe-out of private program rights.
nasa-tm-19700028253-symmetric-round-trip:
G. R. Woodcock of the Advanced Systems Office at the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on September 26, 1969. It studies symmetric round trip flybys to the outer planets. A flyby craft swings past a planet and uses its gravity to bend the flight path, gaining a free change of course.

The analysis first sets out the symmetric flyby concept, pictured for a Jupiter swing. Results tables then give worked missions to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and Pluto in turn. One chart tracks how propulsion needs grow with distance for a five-year Jupiter and Saturn trip. Woodcock closes by recommending where additional study would pay off before such missions were flown.
nasa-tm-19700028267-internal-mobility-ai:
The Space Simulation and Experiments Office at the Marshall Space Flight Center issued this test report on September 12, 1969. It evaluates aids that help astronauts move inside the multiple docking adapter. The adapter was the tunnel-like part of the coming Skylab station where craft docked.

The report gives the methods and steps used in the evaluation. Four different aid concepts were put through the tests. The testing itself was run under contract by the Hayes International Corporation. Handholds, rails, and restraints of this kind decide whether a crew can work smoothly inside a station.
nasa-tm-19710001731-apollo-operations-ha:
NASA's Crew Systems Division issued this volume of the Apollo Operations Handbook for Apollo 14. It describes the extravehicular mobility unit, the spacesuit system that kept astronauts alive on the Moon. Volume One is the system description for that gear.

The unit covers the suit itself and the backpack that feeds it air and cooling. The sample pages show the book's change log in detail. Revisions add a dual-position purge valve and swap hook-and-loop strips for zippers in places. Other changes mark the commander's suit with arm and leg bands. A living handbook like this one kept the flight gear's paper record exact.
nasa-tm-19720005401-effects-of-inhalatio:
Vernon L Carter of NASA in Houston and co-authors from the Air Force and SysteMed Corporation reported this Freon 113 safety study in December 1970, as NASA TM X-67461. Freon 113 was a common refrigerant, solvent, and cleaning agent. Workers breathed it daily, so its long exposure effects needed checking. Earlier work had flagged effects on the human nervous system at higher levels.

Animals lived for fourteen days in a Thomas Dome filled with the gas. The mixed group held monkeys, dogs, mice, and rats. The exposure level was twice the workplace limit then in force. No animals died, and no ill symptoms appeared. Blood values and clinical chemistry also stayed normal. The results supported the view that Freon 113 was fairly safe.
nasa-tm-19720011117-operational-characte:
Walter C Lathem and Wayne R Hudson of the Lewis Research Center reported these thruster tests in January 1972, as NASA TM X-68008. Their subject was a beam steering system for a five centimeter Kaufman ion thruster. A steerable ion beam helps a satellite hold position and attitude. One steering method slides the screen grid sideways to tilt the beam. The team measured how that system behaved.

They recorded beam deflection angle against spring positioning power. They also tracked stray current striking the accelerator grid at each angle. Response time tests timed how fast the beam could swing. Results matched similar measurements made by Hughes Research Laboratories. The agreement between the two labs was good. Such thrusters promised long, gentle pushing in orbit.
new-england-salmon-hatcheries-and-salmon:
Gathered here are seven reports on New England salmon hatcheries and fisheries from the late 1800s. The first, from the United States Fish Commissioner, ran in the Bulletin of the Fish Commission in 1881. It records results from breeding Maine and California salmon in New England and Canada in 1879 and 1880.

Later pieces sketch the Penobscot salmon breeding station in 1883, and the penning of salmon to secure their eggs. Memoranda from Bucksport, on Maine's Penobscot River, describe holding pens from hands on work. Reports follow from Schoodic and Craig Brook, ending with notes on catching Atlantic salmon at sea in 1894.
olalla:
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote this tale of a tainted house in Spain, and it came out in 1885. It was bound in his set The Merry Men, from which this text is drawn. The theme is atavism, the throw back of a line to a brute past in its blood.

A young English man, hurt in war, heals in a lone house in the hills of Spain. The old house holds a fair maid, Olalla, and a mother and son sunk in a strange decay. Dread grows from blood and birth, not from ghosts, in this grave short tale.
our-holidays-their-meaning-and-spirit-re: Our Holidays: Their Meaning and Spirit retells holiday lore for children from St. Nicholas magazine. The Century Company published it in 1906. It belongs to a five-volume set of historical stories for the young. The hosted sample shows the series advertisement and the title page. An illustration there cries Ho, for the Christmas tree. The contents heading follows, and the text stops. No holiday chapter appears in the sample.
podcast-dannyjones-QZxYZUxM9LA:
Comedian Duncan Trussell joins Danny Jones to recount, in his words, going to the billionaire Antichrist lecture. He spins the encounter into a story about wealth and power. At its center stands a figure he presents as a would-be Antichrist instructing the rich. Trussell's telling mixes memoir, comedy, and genuine unease in his signature proportions.

Jones, an old friend in the podcast world, plays straight man while Trussell riffs the anecdote toward theology. How much of the lecture happened as described is a question the episode leaves happily open; Trussell is a storyteller first. What the recording preserves is a beloved comic voice working the exact seam this series mines. That seam is the overlap of elite power and end-times religion. Trussell finds it funny and frightening in the same breath. Listeners get the joke and the shiver together.
podcast-joerogan-rrJhQpvlkLA:
Mike Benz, a former State Department official, briefs Joe Rogan in episode 2237 on what he calls the censorship machine. Benz runs a group that tracks government pressure on online speech. He argues a web of agencies and nonprofits quietly shapes what platforms allow.

Benz traces how anti-disinformation work grew after 2016 into a large, funded system. He names the offices and funding paths he says steer content rules at big platforms. Rogan asks how much of it targets ordinary Americans. The episode gives Benz's full tour of what he calls the blob that governs the internet.
ray-s-daughter-a-story-of-manila:
Ray's Daughter, a story of Manila by General Charles King, U.S.V., author of Ray's Recruit and The Colonel's Daughter, was published at Philadelphia and London by J. B. Lippincott Company in 1901. A frontispiece shows a group gathered about a prostrate form in the pale blue uniform of a Filipino captain, hinting at the war tale to come.

Chapter one, though, opens far from Manila, on a train crossing a western desert at the close of a long June day. Slanting sun beats on the grimy roofs, dust-clouds roll from the wheels in tawny billows, and beyond the sand and sage-brush a flat, ash-colored inland lake spreads to the low ridges.
rescuing-the-czar-two-authentic-diaries-:
James P. Smythe arranged and translated the two diaries that this book presents as authentic, in a third edition of 1920. Part one shares the book's title, Rescuing the Czar. Its first chapter, From Splendor to Gloom, opens on the river Neva in 1917, with the ice breaking up.

At the Winter Palace, ladies rejoice over good news: Bagdad taken, America breaking with the Central Powers, and Lloyd George driving for victory. Then a guard bursts in and puts the women under arrest. The pent-up Revolution has burst, the account says, and the isolated Czar is captive while anarchy howls around the capital.
the-horla:
Guy de Maupassant, a French master of the short tale, wrote this dread work in 1887. It here stands in the English form from the 1907 set of the world's best mystery tales. Maupassant was then at the peak of his craft, and close to the ill health that would claim him.

A man writes in his diary of a being he calls the Horla, which no eye can see. It drinks his milk at night, drains his strength, and bends his will more each day. The tale is a peak of the horror of the mind, where madness and the unseen blur.
the-journal-to-stella:
Jonathan Swift's Journal to Stella appears here in George A. Aitken's edition. Methuen of London published it in 1901. Introduction and notes come with it. Aitken's preface tells the letters' curious history. On Swift's death, twenty-five of them fell to Dr. Lyon. Lyon had charge of Swift in his last years. They passed to a man named Wilkes. They were sold for Hawkesworth's 1766 edition. That editor changed the text freely. He suppressed most of the little language.

The manuscripts reached the British Museum in time. John Forster printed original passages in his Life of Swift. He exposed the tampering plainly. Swift himself had blotted words in later years. Forster restored some of them. Aitken worked from Forster and Ryland's 1897 collation. He examined the tiny, crowded handwriting himself. The edition aims to give the journal as Swift wrote it. Esther Johnson was its Stella.
the-life-of-james-renwick-a-historical-s:
Thomas Houston wrote his sketch of James Renwick as an introduction to Renwick letters, published by Alex. Gardner at Paisley in 1865. A cover picture shows Renwick execution at Edinburgh in 1688. Houston calls him the last and most illustrious of the seventeenth century Scottish martyrs.

His introduction opens with a prophet message to Eli about honor given to those who honor God. Renwick, Houston argues, won lasting honor though rulers in church and state hated and slandered him. The sketch also defends Renwick character and testimony against charges that followed his name for generations.
the-lives-of-the-twelve-caesars-volume-0:
Volume four of Suetonius's Lives, in Alexander Thomson's translation revised by T. Forester, treats Caius Caesar, called Caligula. Suetonius starts with the father, Germanicus, adopted by his uncle Tiberius and rushed through early offices. Sent to Germany after Augustus died, Germanicus faced legions who refused Tiberius and offered to make him emperor instead, and he restored order without betraying his loyalty.

Germanicus then triumphed, conquered the king of Armenia, and made Cappadocia a province. He died at Antioch at thirty-four, of a lingering sickness, not without suspicion of poison, since livid spots appeared all over his body. Beginning with a beloved, possibly murdered father lets Suetonius frame the son's life against what Rome had hoped for.
the-scientific-american-boy-or-the-camp-: A. Russell Bond wrote The Scientific American Boy, or The Camp at Willow Clump Island. Munn and Company published it in New York in 1906. The pages shown give the title matter and the start of the contents only. No chapter text follows. Chapter one is headed with the name Bill in quotation marks. Its topics include an old trunk, Christmas vacation, and a skate sail. Organizing the society at Willow Clump Island is also promised. Chapter two turns to skate sails of several kinds.
the-treaty-held-with-the-indians-of-the-:
Printed at Philadelphia in 1743 and reprinted in London by T. Sowle Raylton and Luke Hinde at sixpence, this Treaty records the conference held with the Indians of the Six Nations at Philadelphia in July 1742. Its preface explains that a copy fell into the editor's hands and seemed to deserve wider knowledge than the few copies sent over from America would give. He first thought of prefixing an account of the customs and manners of these people, drawn from printed relations and his own correspondence.

Instead, the pamphlet prefixes an account of the first confederacy of the Six Nations, their tributaries, dependents, and allies. The treaty speeches themselves follow, a formal record of Iroquois diplomacy with Pennsylvania. Students of early American history get both the proceedings and an English bookseller's sense that colonial Indian affairs mattered to readers at home.
the-voyage-of-captain-popanilla: Benjamin Disraeli's Voyage of Captain Popanilla was first published in 1827, as an editorial line in both library records of the tale notes. This record presents only that heading and a bare contents list of eighteen numbered chapters, so the voyage itself does not appear. No chapter titles are given, and no narrative wording accompanies the list. A companion record of the same work opens directly with chapter one and its island in the Indian Ocean. This entry confirms the authorship, first publication date, and chapter count.
un-doc-international-review-of-criminal-:
Harmonizing criminal law across borders is the subject of a chapter in the International Review of Criminal Policy, issues 43 and 44, a United Nations journal on crime and justice. The chapter appeared in the early 1980s. It looks at how states write their penal codes in very different ways.

Inside, the chapter argues that closer alignment of crime laws would help states cooperate. Shared definitions make joint work on offenders and evidence far easier. Readers get a clear view of an early push for common ground in criminal law, long before such talks became routine.
ursula:
Honore de Balzac wrote Ursula, and Katharine Prescott Wormeley made this English rendering. He dedicated the novel to his niece Sophie Surville. Winning a young girl's approval, he told her, was a true pleasure for a writer. Girls must be kept from books less pure than their own souls. Chapter one, The Frightened Heirs, opens at Nemours, on the road from Paris. There the town crosses the canal du Loing.

Balzac paints the town before the plot starts. Steep canal banks serve as walls and as walks. A small suburb has grown past the bridge since 1830. He fixes the scene in 1829, when Nemours still kept its graceful old look. The frightened heirs of the title wait in the wings. Readers meet one of Balzac's studies of greed, family, and a young woman's fate, set in a place he renders street by street.
